topic: Day 1 · Diagnosing DKA — The Triad, Severity & the Euglycaemic Trap
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Acute Medical Unit
speakerBio: An acute physician who has watched too many euglycaemic DKAs walk out of the department reassured, and now teaches every trainee to check a ketone before they trust a sugar. His motto: the glucometer is a comforting liar.
lectureHTML:
🎯 Where we start — 21:10, majors cubicle 4

Two patients arrive within ten minutes. The first is a 24-year-old with type 1 diabetes: glucose 28 mmol/L, breathing deeply, vomiting. The second is a 38-year-old woman, 30 weeks pregnant, started on an SGLT2 inhibitor for weight — nauseated, breathless, unwell, and her capillary glucose is 7.9 mmol/L — completely normal. One of these is an obvious DKA. The other is a DKA that will be missed by every clinician who trusts the glucose. By the end of this session you will diagnose both in under a minute — and you will never again be reassured by a normal sugar.

1 · The one sentence that holds the session

DKA is diagnosed on a triad, not on a glucose. If you can only remember one thing: ketones and acid make the diagnosis; the glucose merely raises the suspicion.

Session 1 built the machine. This session turns it into a bedside diagnosis you can make from a venous gas and a capillary ketone in seconds — then grades how sick the patient is, and disarms the single most dangerous trap in the whole field: the DKA that presents with a normal blood sugar.

2 · The diagnostic triad — all three, every time 🔺

The diagnosis of DKA (per the Joint British Diabetes Societies, JBDS-IP) requires all three of the following. Miss one and you are not diagnosing DKA.

LimbThresholdNote
1. Hyperglycaemia (D)Glucose >11 mmol/L (>200 mg/dL) — or known diabetes mellitus"Or known diabetes" is deliberate — it is what admits euglycaemic DKA. The glucose can be normal.
2. Ketonaemia / ketosis (K)Capillary BHB ≥3 mmol/L, or urine ketones ≥2+ on dipstickCapillary BHB is the modern standard — it measures the dominant ketone directly.
3. Acidosis (A)pH <7.3 and/or bicarbonate <15 mmol/LA venous gas is sufficient — no need for an arterial sample. This is the "acid" that defines danger.
D-K-A: the name is the diagnosis. D for hyperglycaemia (Diabetes/Deranged glucose), K for Ketones, A for Acidosis. All three, confirmed on a venous gas plus a capillary ketone.
💡 Pearl — a venous gas is enough

You do not need an arterial blood gas to diagnose or monitor DKA. Venous pH runs ~0.02–0.04 lower than arterial and venous bicarbonate correlates closely — entirely adequate for diagnosis and for tracking resolution. Spare the patient repeated arterial stabs; a venous gas gives you pH, bicarbonate, potassium and glucose in one 60-second sample. Repeat it, plus capillary BHB, to track progress.

3 · Grading severity — the JBDS markers 📊

Not all DKA is equal. The JBDS defines features that mark severe DKA and mandate consideration of HDU/ICU-level care, senior review, and closer monitoring. The presence of any one of these should raise your level of concern and care.

Marker of severity (JBDS)ThresholdWhy it matters
Blood ketones (BHB)>6 mmol/LVery high acid load / substrate.
Bicarbonate<5 mmol/LBicarbonate nearly exhausted — severe acidosis.
Venous/arterial pH<7.1Profound acidaemia; risk of cardiovascular compromise.
Potassium on admission<3.5 mmol/LLife-threatening — insulin will drop it further; needs replacement before insulin.
GCSReduced (GCS <12) or abnormal AVPUCerebral effect / airway risk.
Oxygen saturationLow on airConcomitant pathology (aspiration, pneumonia, ARDS).
Systolic BP<90 mmHgShock / profound volume depletion.
Pulse>100 or <60 bpmMarked tachycardia (shock) or ominous bradycardia (peri-arrest / severe electrolyte disturbance).
Anion gap>16Confirms/quantifies the high-anion-gap acidosis.
⚠️ Danger — potassium below 3.5 on admission

A presenting potassium <3.5 mmol/L is a red flag that overrides the usual sequence. Total-body potassium is already severely depleted, and if you start insulin it will drive the serum potassium lower still, into arrhythmia. In this situation potassium replacement (and often HDU/ICU care) must precede or accompany insulin, and insulin may need to be delayed until potassium is being replaced and is safely above 3.5. This single number can change the entire order of your first ten minutes.

4 · The euglycaemic DKA trap — the most important slide of the day ☠️

Here is the pitfall that will, sooner or later, put a patient in danger if you do not internalise it now. Euglycaemic DKA is a genuine, full ketoacidosis — all the acid, all the ketones, all the risk — but with a normal or only mildly raised blood glucose (often <11 mmol/L). The triad still holds because the hyperglycaemia limb is satisfied by "or known diabetes". The mechanism: some factor either lowers glucose or limits its rise while insulin deficiency (relative or absolute) still permits full-blown ketogenesis.

Cause of euglycaemic DKAWhy the glucose stays (near) normal
SGLT2 inhibitors (–gliflozins)They dump glucose in the urine (glucosuria), holding the plasma glucose down while insulin deficiency/illness still drives ketogenesis. The classic modern cause — flagged by the MHRA/FDA. Suspect in any unwell patient on a gliflozin.
PregnancyIncreased glucose utilisation by the foetus and accelerated starvation ketosis; pregnant women develop DKA at lower glucose and faster.
Starvation / poor intake / vomitingLow glycogen and gluconeogenic substrate limit the glucose rise while lipolysis/ketogenesis proceed.
Alcohol (alcoholic ketoacidosis)Alcohol impairs gluconeogenesis (high NADH) — ketosis with normal or low glucose.
Reduced insulin dose / sick-day error, liver diseaseEnough context for ketogenesis without the expected hyperglycaemia.
⚠️ Danger — do NOT be reassured by the glucose

The single sentence to carry out of this conference: a normal blood glucose does not exclude DKA. If a patient — especially one on an SGLT2 inhibitor, pregnant, alcohol-dependent, or starved — is unwell, vomiting, breathless or acidotic, check capillary ketones and a venous gas regardless of the glucose. Countless euglycaemic DKAs are sent home or managed as "gastroenteritis" because the sugar looked fine. The glucometer is the most reassuring liar in the department.

💡 Pearl — SGLT2 inhibitors and surgery

Because SGLT2 inhibitors precipitate euglycaemic DKA, guidance is to withhold them during acute illness, before surgery (typically ~3 days pre-op), and during any period of reduced oral intake or dehydration ("sick-day rules"). A perioperative euglycaemic DKA with a normal sugar is a classic, dangerous, and entirely preventable event.

5 · Differentials of a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis 🔬

DKA is one cause of a raised-anion-gap metabolic acidosis (HAGMA). When the picture is atypical — no diabetes history, ketones modest, glucose normal — run the differential. The classic mnemonic is GOLD MARK (or the older MUDPILES).

Letter (GOLD MARK)Cause
GGlycols (ethylene glycol, propylene glycol)
OOxoproline (5-oxoproline, chronic paracetamol)
LL-lactate (sepsis, hypoperfusion, metformin)
DD-lactate (short-gut)
MMethanol
AAspirin (salicylates)
RRenal failure (uraemia)
KKetoacidosis — diabetic, alcoholic, or starvation

Anion gap = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻), normal ~8–12 mmol/L (higher without potassium in the formula). A gap >16 with ketones and the right context is DKA; a high gap without ketones should send you hunting through the rest of GOLD MARK — lactate, toxic alcohols, salicylates and uraemia in particular.

🎯 Ketoacidosis is not only diabetic

Three ketoacidoses share the same final pathway: diabetic (insulin deficiency), alcoholic (starvation + alcohol impairing gluconeogenesis, often with a near-normal glucose), and starvation (usually mild, bicarbonate rarely <18). Alcoholic ketoacidosis in particular presents with high ketones, a raised anion gap, and a normal or low glucose — it is a euglycaemic ketoacidosis in a non-diabetic, treated with glucose and thiamine and fluids, not insulin.

6 · Point-of-care ketone monitoring — the tool that runs the whole admission 🩸

The bedside capillary beta-hydroxybutyrate meter has transformed DKA care. It is your diagnostic test and your monitor of treatment response.

  • Diagnosis: BHB ≥3 mmol/L satisfies the ketosis limb of the triad in seconds.
  • Monitoring: the target during treatment is a fall in BHB of at least 0.5 mmol/L per hour (Session 4). A ketone meter, repeated hourly, tells you whether your insulin is actually clearing the acid.
  • Resolution: DKA is resolved when BHB <0.6 mmol/L, pH >7.3 and bicarbonate >15 — driven primarily by the ketone, because that is the disease.
  • Why not urine ketones? Urine dipsticks measure acetoacetate only, lag behind the blood, and — as covered in Session 1 — can rise as the patient improves. Blood BHB is the standard.
Diagnose with the triad, grade with the JBDS markers, and let the capillary ketone drive every decision from admission to resolution.
☠️ M&M — "Sugar's normal, must be a chest infection"

A 41-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, recently started on empagliflozin, presented with three days of nausea, malaise and breathlessness before a planned laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Her capillary glucose was 8.6 mmol/L. She was labelled a likely chest infection, given oral antibiotics and listed to proceed. Post-induction she became profoundly acidotic; the gas showed pH 7.02, bicarbonate 6, and blood ketones 5.8 mmol/L — euglycaemic DKA precipitated by an SGLT2 inhibitor continued through pre-operative starvation. No one had checked a ketone because the sugar was normal, and the drug had not been withheld before surgery. She survived after ICU admission and an insulin/dextrose infusion. Lessons: (1) a normal glucose never excludes DKA — check capillary ketones in any unwell patient on a gliflozin; (2) withhold SGLT2 inhibitors during acute illness and before surgery; (3) breathlessness in a diabetic may be Kussmaul breathing, not a chest infection. The glucometer told a comforting lie and everyone believed it.

7 · Take-home 🎯

  • Triad (D-K-A): hyperglycaemia >11 mmol/L (or known diabetes) + ketones (BHB ≥3 / urine ≥2+) + acidosis (pH <7.3 or bicarbonate <15). All three.
  • Diagnose and monitor on a venous gas plus capillary BHB — no arterial stab needed.
  • Grade severity by the JBDS markers: BHB >6, pH <7.1, bicarbonate <5, K⁺ <3.5 on admission, GCS drop, low sats, SBP <90, pulse >100 or <60, anion gap >16 → senior/HDU-ICU.
  • Euglycaemic DKA is real: SGLT2 inhibitors, pregnancy, starvation, alcohol → full ketoacidosis with a normal sugar. Never be reassured by the glucose.
  • A high-anion-gap acidosis without ketones → work through GOLD MARK (lactate, toxic alcohols, salicylates, uraemia).
  • The capillary BHB meter diagnoses, monitors (target fall ≥0.5 mmol/L/h) and confirms resolution (BHB <0.6).

Next session: with the diagnosis made, the first therapeutic pillar — fluid resuscitation. Why refilling the tank drops the glucose before insulin even acts, the JBDS regimen, the corrected-sodium warning, and the cerebral-oedema catastrophe you must never cause.

moderatorQs.q: A 30-week-pregnant woman on an SGLT2 inhibitor is unwell and acidotic with a capillary glucose of 7.9 mmol/L. Walk me through how she can still have DKA when her sugar is normal.
moderatorQs.answerHTML: She has euglycaemic DKA, and she satisfies the diagnostic triad because the hyperglycaemia limb reads 'glucose >11 mmol/L or known diabetes' — the glucose need not be high. Two forces keep her sugar down while ketogenesis runs unchecked: the SGLT2 inhibitor is spilling glucose into her urine (glucosuria), capping the plasma glucose, and pregnancy increases foetal glucose consumption and accelerates starvation ketosis, so pregnant women ketose faster and at lower glucose. Meanwhile relative insulin deficiency plus the stress of illness still permits full lipolysis and hepatic ketogenesis, producing a genuine high-anion-gap ketoacidosis. The lesson: confirm the diagnosis on capillary BHB (≥3 mmol/L) and a venous gas (pH <7.3, bicarbonate <15), never on the glucose — and treat with insulin plus dextrose to keep the sugar up while clearing the ketones.

moderatorQs.q: You have diagnosed DKA. The admission potassium is 3.2 mmol/L. Why does that number change your immediate plan, and what do you do?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: A presenting potassium of 3.2 mmol/L is a JBDS marker of severe DKA and a specific red flag that overrides the normal sequence. Total-body potassium is already severely depleted, and giving insulin — which drives K⁺ into cells — would push the serum level lower still, straight into the range that causes fatal ventricular arrhythmia. So the plan changes: do not start insulin yet; give fluids and replace potassium first (with the patient on a cardiac monitor, in an HDU/ICU setting), and only begin the fixed-rate insulin infusion once potassium is being actively replaced and is safely above 3.5 mmol/L. It is one of the few situations where you deliberately delay insulin in DKA — because the potassium will kill faster than the acid.

moderatorQs.q: A patient has a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis but only trivial ketones and no diabetes. How do you think through the differential?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: I first confirm and quantify the gap — anion gap = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻), abnormal above ~12–16 — then, because the ketones are trivial, I deliberately step off DKA and work through GOLD MARK: Glycols (ethylene/propylene glycol), Oxoproline (chronic paracetamol), L-lactate (sepsis, hypoperfusion, metformin), D-lactate, Methanol, Aspirin/salicylates, Renal failure/uraemia, and Ketoacidosis (which also includes alcoholic and starvation, both of which can be near-euglycaemic). Practically I would send a lactate, renal function, salicylate and paracetamol levels, an osmolar gap (raised in toxic-alcohol poisoning), and a careful history for alcohol and ingestions. The key discipline is that a raised gap without ketones is not DKA until proven, and the toxic alcohols and salicylates are time-critical, treatable diagnoses you must not miss.

audienceQs.q: Do I really need an arterial blood gas to diagnose and monitor DKA, or can I use a venous one?
audienceQs.answerHTML: A venous blood gas is sufficient for both diagnosing and monitoring DKA — you do not need to keep taking arterial samples. Venous pH runs only about 0.02–0.04 lower than arterial, and venous bicarbonate correlates closely enough for clinical decisions; both comfortably capture the acidosis limb of the triad (pH <7.3, bicarbonate <15). A single venous sample gives you pH, bicarbonate, potassium and glucose together, which is exactly what you need to start and titrate treatment. Repeat the venous gas alongside a capillary BHB to track resolution. Reserve arterial sampling for when you specifically need accurate oxygenation or pCO₂ — for example a patient with concurrent respiratory failure — not for routine DKA monitoring.

audienceQs.q: Our trust is starting more patients on SGLT2 inhibitors. What counselling reduces the risk of the euglycaemic DKA you described?
audienceQs.answerHTML: The core message is sick-day rules and perioperative withholding. Counsel patients to stop the SGLT2 inhibitor during any acute illness — vomiting, diarrhoea, significant infection, dehydration, or reduced food intake — and to restart only once they are eating and drinking normally and well again. For planned surgery it should be withheld for around 3 days before the procedure (regimen varies, follow local guidance) to avoid a perioperative euglycaemic DKA during the starvation period. Warn them that symptoms of DKA — nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, breathlessness, malaise — can occur even when their home glucose readings look normal, and that these symptoms warrant urgent ketone testing and medical review rather than reassurance. Also flag the increased risk with very low carbohydrate diets and heavy alcohol. Clear, written sick-day guidance at the point of prescribing prevents most of these events.

audienceQs.q: When should I be doing a capillary ketone rather than waiting for the doctor to ask for one?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Have a very low threshold — a capillary ketone takes seconds and catches the DKAs that a glucose alone misses. Check one on any patient with known diabetes who is unwell (vomiting, abdominal pain, breathless, drowsy, or febrile), on any acidotic or deeply/rapidly breathing patient, and crucially on any unwell patient taking an SGLT2 inhibitor, who is pregnant, alcohol-dependent or clearly not eating — regardless of what the glucose shows, because these are the euglycaemic DKAs. A BHB of 3 mmol/L or more flags likely DKA and should prompt an immediate venous gas and doctor review; even 1–3 mmol/L in an unwell patient warrants escalation. In short: if they are a diabetic and they are sick, or they are acidotic, do the ketone before you trust the sugar.
